summary: This experimental document defines an alternate tunnel encapsulation for data frames in CAPWAP, the protocol that lets a controller manage wireless access points. A station's 802.11 data frames can either be bridged locally or tunneled to the controller. The extension offers another way to encapsulate tunneled frames.

eli5.summary: Wi-Fi boxes in a building can pass messages to a main boss box inside a tube. This describes another kind of tube you can use.

subtitle: Let wireless access points tunnel data through multiple paths instead of always to the controller.

tldr.problem: CAPWAP manages wireless access points (WTPs) through a central controller (AC), but existing tunnel modes force all user traffic through the controller. This limits scalability and flexibility when different network operators manage the controller and access network.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds message elements that let an access point negotiate and support multiple tunnel encapsulation types (CAPWAP, GRE, PMIPv6, IP-in-IP, and others) to send data frames to a different endpoint, such as an access router, while keeping control traffic to the AC.
tldr.outcome: Access points can now separate the data plane from the control plane, scaling independently. The extension is Experimental and designed for carrier-grade Wi-Fi networks and multi-tenant environments.

today: RFC 8350 is an Experimental RFC. It documents an extension to CAPWAP that has been tested by service providers seeking scalable solutions for large Wi-Fi networks. The specification remains experimental pending wider deployment and operational feedback.

sections.title: The CAPWAP Architecture
sections.content:
CAPWAP is a protocol for a central controller (AC) to manage wireless access points (WTPs) distributed across a network. Each WTP handles radio traffic from stations while the AC manages policy and configuration.

By default, CAPWAP separates control messages from data frames. The control channel carries management traffic in both directions. For user data, the existing standard offers three modes: local bridging at the WTP, or tunneling all frames back to the AC in either IEEE 802.3 or IEEE 802.11 format.

In local bridging mode, each WTP sends user traffic directly to its connected access router, reducing load on the AC. However, this prevents the AC from applying policy to the data. When tunneling is needed, the RFC now allows data to go to a different endpoint and use different encapsulation.
sections.eli5: The Wi-Fi box can learn to send some packages to the nearest mail sorter instead of all the way to the main office. The main office still tells it what to do, but the data takes a shortcut.

sections.title: Why Alternate Tunneling
sections.content:
Large service providers deploy hundreds of thousands of access points generating enormous data traffic. Centralizing all data at one controller creates a bottleneck.

The RFC addresses two key scenarios. First, when the WTP operator differs from the access network operator, policy enforcement must happen in the WTP operator's network, not at an external router. Second, many encapsulation types (L2TP, GRE, IP-in-IP) exist and are widely deployed; operators want to leverage these instead of being forced to use only CAPWAP.

The extension supports Virtual Network Operators (VNOs) that lease WTP resources from a provider. By assigning different SSIDs to different VNOs, each SSID's traffic can be tunneled to that VNO's access router via the appropriate encapsulation, all under one AC's control.
sections.eli5: Different delivery companies need their packages to go to different warehouses, and they prefer tubes they already use instead of learning new ones.

sections.title: Tunnel Types and Setup
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven tunnel encapsulation types: CAPWAP, L2TP, L2TPv3, IP-in-IP, PMIPv6-UDP, GRE, and GTPv1-U. For each, the controller can specify the tunnel endpoint (an access router address), optional encryption policy, quality-of-service tagging, and transport protocol (UDP or UDP-Lite for CAPWAP).

Setup follows a standard CAPWAP flow. When the WTP joins the controller, it announces which tunnel types it can support using a new Supported Alternate Tunnel Encapsulations message element. The controller responds with the selected type in an IEEE 802.11 Add WLAN configuration message, carrying tunnel-specific parameters like the access router addresses and any optional elements (GRE keys, DTLS encryption flags, tagging policy).

The WTP then establishes the alternate tunnel and reports success. If the tunnel fails, the WTP informs the controller so it can reconfigure the WLAN or fall back to local bridging or the standard CAPWAP tunnel.
sections.eli5: The Wi-Fi box tells the boss what tubes it can use. The boss picks one and tells the box where the tube goes and how to use it. The box hooks up the tube and tells the boss it is ready.

sections.title: Information Elements and Parameters
sections.content:
The extension adds six new message elements to CAPWAP. The Supported Alternate Tunnel Encapsulations element carries a list of tunnel-type codes the WTP supports. The Alternate Tunnel Encapsulations Type element is sent by the controller with the selected type and a variable-length Info Element field containing tunnel-specific sub-elements.

For CAPWAP-based tunnels, sub-elements include the access router address (IPv4 or IPv6), a Tunnel DTLS Policy for encryption (matching the AC's policy), an IEEE 802.11 Tagging Mode for QoS (IEEE 802.1p or DSCP), and a CAPWAP Transport Protocol selector (UDP or UDP-Lite). GRE tunnels add a GRE Key Element. PMIPv6 tunnels need only the access router address. An IPv6 MTU Element communicates the minimum MTU for IPv6-based tunnels. The third new message element is the IEEE 802.11 WTP Alternate Tunnel Failure Indication, which reports tunnel failures or recovery by WLAN ID, affected access routers, and a status flag.
sections.eli5: The box lists what tubes it knows. The boss says which tube to use and how, giving addresses and settings. The box can say if the tube breaks.

sections.title: Deployment and Multi-Tenant Support
sections.content:
The VNO scenario best shows the extension's value. A single WTP advertises multiple SSIDs; each SSID belongs to a different virtual operator. The controller assigns each SSID a different tunnel type and endpoint address. Traffic for SSID1 goes via CAPWAP to VNO-1's access router. Traffic for SSID2 goes via GRE to VNO-2's access router, all signaled by one AC.

For reliability, the controller can list multiple access router addresses for load balancing or redundancy. The WTP selects among them and reports which one it is using. If an access router becomes unavailable, the WTP notifies the AC and can fall back to another address or to local bridging.

Control traffic always flows to the central AC via CAPWAP Control and Data Channels, so the AC maintains full visibility and control over the WTP and its management functions, including IEEE 802.11 action frames. Only the user data plane is decoupled.
sections.eli5: One boss manages many shops. Each shop's packages go to that shop's warehouse via the tube that warehouse uses. If a warehouse is down, packages go to a backup warehouse.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The new message elements travel in CAPWAP Control messages, inheriting CAPWAP's authentication and protection mechanisms. The specification does not introduce new security risks to the control plane compared to the base CAPWAP protocol.

In the data plane, security depends on the selected encapsulation type. If the encapsulation type itself is not secured (for example, basic IP-in-IP), operators are advised to protect the tunnel using IPsec or other known secure methods. The RFC is Experimental; implementations are expected to verify the approach before standardization.
